The table at hand is an extract from the “MAXIMA Superposition” manual’s Table of Contents. It spans two principal chapters—“Theoretical Principles” and “Input Description”—and is organized into three columns:  
  1. Section Number (hierarchical numbering with major, minor, and sub-sub items)  
  2. Section Title (the name or topic of each section)  
  3. Page Reference (right-aligned, indicates where the section begins)

Structure and Hierarchy  
• Major Sections (Level 1) appear in bold and carry numbers “2” and “3.”  
  – 2 Theoretical Principles (starts page 2-1)  
  – 3 Input Description (starts page 3-1)  

• Subsections (Level 2) list detailed topics under each major heading, indented one level. For example, under “2 Theoretical Principles” there is:  
  – 2.1 General Information (page 2-1)  
  – 2.2 Combinations according to EN 1990 as well as the National Annexes and DIN-Fachbericht (page 2-2)  
  – 2.3 Superposition with Explicit Defined Combination (page 2-4)  
  – 2.4 Simplified Superpositions (page 2-5)  
  – 2.5 Superposition without any Partial Safety Factors and Coefficients (page 2-7)  
  – 2.6 Superposition of Non-linearly Analysed Load Cases (page 2-7)  
  – 2.7 Intermediate Superposition (page 2-7)  
  – 2.8 Modification of Partial Safety Factors and Combination Coefficients (page 2-10)

• Sub-subsections (Level 3) further break down complex topics. Under 2.2 and 2.4 and 2.7 these include:  
  – 2.2.1 Fundamental Combinations according to Equations 6.10 and 6.10a+6.10b (page 2-2)  
  – 2.2.2 Accidental Combinations (2-3), 2.2.3 Seismic Combination (2-3), 2.2.4 Combinations for Checks of the Serviceability (2-3)  
  – 2.4.1 Ultimate Limit State Check: Fundamental Combination (2-6), 2.4.2 Ultimate Limit State Check: Accidental Combination (2-6), 2.4.3 Serviceability Limit State Check: Characteristic (Rare) Combination (2-6)  
  – 2.7.1 Intermediate Superposition using Load Groups (2-7), 2.7.2 Input Example: Hangar with Seismic Design (2-7)

Under Chapter 3 (“Input Description”), the structure is similar:  
• 3.1 Input Language (3-1)  
• 3.2 Input Records (3-2)  
• 3.3 Design Codes and Recommended Combinations (3-8) with eleven sub-items enumerating various international standards:  
  – 3.3.1 EN – Eurocodes (3-8)  
  – 3.3.2 DIN – Deutsche Norm (3-8)  
  – 3.3.3 OEN – Österreichische Norm (3-9)  
  – 3.3.4 SIA – Schweizer Norm (3-10)  
  – 3.3.5 BS – British Standard and ZA – South African Standard (3-10)  
  – 3.3.6 US – American Standards and Unified Building Code (3-11)  
  – 3.3.7 SP – Russian Standard (3-11)  
  – 3.3.8 IS – Indian Standard (3-11)  
  – 3.3.9 AS – Australian Standard and NZS – New Zealand Standard (3-12)  
  – 3.3.10 UNE – Instrucciones Española (3-12)  
  – 3.3.11 UNI – Decreto Ministeriale Italiane (3-12)

Key Observations for RAG Indexing  
• Hierarchical IDs enable precise section retrieval (e.g., “2.4.2” directly maps to the ULS accidental combination rule).  
• Titles are brisk but descriptive; they can serve as metadata keys in a vector store.  
• Page numbers can be used for chunking or bounding the PDF extraction.  
• The pattern of dotted leaders links titles to pages, which is consistent across levels—ideal for automated parsing.  

This detailed breakdown supports building a structured knowledge graph or vector-based index where each section and subsection becomes a retrievable node, enriched by its title, hierarchy, and location in the source manual.

Dot-leader lines fill the gap between columns 2 and 3. Indentation of the section numbers and their captions encodes hierarchy (top-level sections have no indent, first-level subsections are indented slightly, second-level more so, etc.).

Key characteristics for RAG/QA indexing:  
  • Each row is a distinct retrievable topic with unique section ID.  
  • The dot-leaders can be stripped away; the three logical fields are Section, Title, Page.  
  • Indentation level implies parent–child relationships (useful for hierarchical queries).  
  • Page references use a “chapter‐page” format (e.g. “3-40” means Chapter 3, page 40).  
  • Many entries use “Literal” or three‐letter abbreviations (COMB, ACT, ADD, ADA, LC, SUPP, etc.)—these are command keywords within the MAXIMA Superposition DSL.  

By parsing out (SectionID, Title, Page, Level) for each line, one can build a vector‐store index that supports fine‐grained retrieval: e.g. “Where is the definition of literal TYPE?” returns (3.6.2, “Literal TYPE – Type of the result load cases”, 3-21).

The results which were calculated with the SOFiSTiK programs are stored in the database. The task of the program MAXIMA is the determination of extreme values of the internal forces, stresses, displacements, support reactions and results of result sets.
 Different methods according to the partial safety concepts of the Eurocode and international design codes and according to the conventional method without partial safety factors can be used to determine the maximum values. Here MAXIMA finds the most unfavourable action effect and applies the combination factors automatically.
 To achieve this, the superposition is done in two steps. In the inner step MAXIMA finds the extreme value from different load cases of the action effect and in a second outer process the action effects are combined.
 The load cases to be superimposed may be defined unconditionally (e.g. dead load) or condi- tionally (e.g. live load). In a conditional superposition each load case is only applied if it has an unfavourable contribution. The definition of loads which exclude each other (alternate loads) or of loads with changing sign is also possible.
 The load cases which are used for the superposition can be combined through arbitrary com- binations of the calculated load cases. This occurs via the definition of subsequent load cases, which leads to an absolute superposition with the previous load cases. Each load case may be multiplied with a scaling factor, so that normalised loads can be used during the static analysis.
 The loads of non-linearly calculated load cases have to be include already the correspond- ing combination coefficients and safeties. A superposition with action effects (record ACT) is therefore not implemented. However, it is possible to make an alternative selection via the load cases only (record LC). Load cases which have been analysed non-linearly can only be superimposed as individual alternate load cases (TYPE AG1) with the factor 1.
 The results are printed and stored in the database for later design or visualisation purposes. The extent of the output can mainly be controlled by the user. It is recommended to print only the decisive or manually selected parts of the superposition.

Load cases which have been analysed non-linearly can only be superimposed as individual alternate load cases (TYPE AG1) with the factor 1.. The results are printed and stored in the database for later design or visualisation purposes. The extent of the output can mainly be controlled by the user. It is recommended to print only the decisive or manually selected parts of the superposition..
 The user should check the superposition by investigating random samples! With the input of LOAD and FACT in record ECHO all the defined and determined factors and the used load cases are output for every individual superposition value. Only the relevant superposition values are printed with all involved factors, if ECHO CHCK is input.

The superposition rule is determined via the definition of the design code in program AQUA (record NORM) or for the interactive input with SSD or SOFiPLUS at the beginning. MAXIMA then automatically uses the design code which is available in the database. The combination rules of the design codes as well as the National Annexes of the EN 1990 are different. For example, the EN 1990 with its National Annexes provides action combinations with safety and combination coefficients. In contrast, old standards such as DIN 1045 (1988) only combine load cases.
 The actions are already defined before the input of the loads in program SOFiLOAD or with the Action Manager in SSD. The corresponding load cases have to be allocated to the actions. The action can be only modified temporarily in MAXIMA. The superposition is done with partial safety factors and combination coefficients only for actions defined by arbitrary load cases. These load cases or combinations of them will be superimposed to define an action effect.
 A superposition contains all action effects which are defined by a combination rule with the record COMB.
 The most unfavourable variable action is designated as the leading variable action. MAXIMA selects the most unfavourable one and considers it according to the chosen combination rule. When using the explicit defined combination with action groups the determination of three leading variable actions is possible.
 The leading variable actions are marked with a * at sumQ1/sumQ2/sumQ3 (sum of the loads leading variable action) in the output with ECHO FACT FULL. This variable action which has the largest difference between sumL (sum of the loads leading variable action) and sumQI (sum of the loads acting variable) is used as leading variable action! The remaining variable actions are multiplied with the combination coefficient for the accompanying variable action in dependence on the combination rule.
 The default equations 2.1 till 2.7 correspond to the combinations which are given in the EN 1990 (except for equation 6.10a and 6.10b) and in the DIN 1055-100 / DIN-Fachberichte. For the special equations 6.10a and 6.10b of the EN 1990 and their use variants in the National Annexes it is recommended to use the explicit defined combinations.

The default equations 2.1 till 2.7 correspond to the combinations which are given in the EN 1990 (except for equation 6.10a and 6.10b) and in the DIN 1055-100 / DIN-Fachberichte. For the special equations 6.10a and 6.10b of the EN 1990 and their use variants in the National Annexes it is recommended to use the explicit defined combinations..
 For design codes, which are used other equations for the combinations e.g. BS 8110, BS 5400, Australian Standard, Indian Standard, US Standards, it is recommeded to use the explicit defined combination.
 If superposition defaults are available in the INI file for the selected design code, these defaults are used then in MAXIMA without input for COMB, ACT, ADD, LC and SUPP or in the SSD tasks Combination Rules and Superpositioning for Combination Rules. Precondition for this is the usage of the default actions of the record ACT (SOFiLOAD) or of the Loadcase Manager.
 You can find further explanations and examples for different design codes in our Online Help -> Tutorials
 https://www.sofistik.de/documentation/2025/en/tutorials/superpositions/superposition.html
 The number of processable load cases is limited to 999999. Upon request, the user can re- peatedly overwrite previously stored load cases or can recombine the load cases from different databases with DBINFO or DBMERG.
 The results can be stored under a new load case number. Possible available results of former calculations are deleted, unless, something else is requested with the input CTRL DELE.
 The superposition is made separately for each node and for each element or beam or design element section in the database.
 The superposition takes place for all nodes or elements even when not all of them have been selected. However, only the results for the selected nodes or elements are printed out. For special cases it is possible to make a selective superposition with the input SUPP OPT S.
 When the values to be superimposed are close to zero, then some problems arise for the imposed loads, in the calculation of the corresponding internal forces. This is handled by the program MAXIMA in the following manner: If the actual absolute value is less than 10E-6 of the maximum value of all load cases encountered, then the imposed load cases do not participate in the superposition.

When the values to be superimposed are close to zero, then some problems arise for the imposed loads, in the calculation of the corresponding internal forces. This is handled by the program MAXIMA in the following manner: If the actual absolute value is less than 10E-6 of the maximum value of all load cases encountered, then the imposed load cases do not participate in the superposition..
 If however the derivation of the quantity being superimposed is known, e.g. the shear force in the case of a superimposed bending moment, then an imposed load case is used if the corresponding derivation is positive.

Fundamental Combinations according to Equations 6.10 and 6.10a+6.10b
 The following combinations can be used for the superposition and are selectable via the record COMB:
 Fundamental combination for the ultimate limit state (EN 1990 equation 6.10):
 EN 1990 equation 6.10b
 $$Eqa=E Sig. Ge (r) YPA*PK (r) YA-Ad (c) W1,1degQk,1(r) S02,1deg Qk, i (2.2) Jel i>1$$
 The partial safety factor γg,A for the permanent actions and γA for the accidental actions is determined with the input GAMA in record ACT. The default for both partial safety factors is defined in dependence on the selected design code in the INI file and is automatically available.
 The EN 1990 plans the use of ψ2,1 · Qk,1 (= all variable actions with ψ2) as a second variant for the accidental design combination. This variant has to be done with the explicit defined combination COMB EXTR EXPL. An input variant is for example:
 COMB 1 EXTR EXPL TYPE ACCI BASE 3100
 ADD A FACU GAMA FACF 0.0
 ADD G
 FACU GAMA FACF GAMA
 ADD G = FACU GAMA FACF GAMA
 ADD QI FACU PSI2 FACF 0.0
 ADD QI FACU PSI2 FACF 0.0

Seismic combination for the ultimate limit state:
 Frequent combination for the serviceability limit state:
 An input for the explicit defined combination with permanent and variable actions, where only Q, W and S should be used as variable actions, reads for example:
 COMB 1 EXTR EXPL TYPE DESI
 ADD {G} FACU GAM ADD {Q1} FACU GAMU FACF 0.0 ADA Q,W,S ADD {QI} FACU PSI0 FACF 0.0 ADA Q,W,S
 ADD {G} FACU GAM
 ADA Q,W,S
 The definition is done here via action groups, where it is defined at {Q1} that a leading variable action is available. The leading variable action is considered in the unfavourable case with the corresponding partial safety factor γ. The following actions {QI} get only the combination coefficient ψ0 as unfavourable factor.
 Another possibility is to prescribe a special action as leading variable action (e.g. according to French BAEL). A possible input with single actions is for example according to BAEL (D2.2,1 design resistance for buildings, first line of the table):
 COMB 1 EXPL TYPE DESI
 ADD G FACU GAM ADD QB FACU 1.5 FACF 0.0 $leading variable action$ ADD W FACU PSIU FACF 0.0 ADD S FACU PSIU FACF 0.0 ADD T_1 FACU 0.8 FACF 0.0
 The leading variable action is here QB with the factor (γ) 1.5 in the unfavourable case. The accomanying variable actions W and S are considered with the factor γ·ψ0 in the unfavourable case and T_1 with 0.8.
 For a combination which uses ADD it is also possible to input together actions and action groups. For example it is useful, if a specific variable action is the leading variable action and all other defined variable actions are the accompanying variable actions. With the input:

The accomanying variable actions W and S are considered with the factor γ·ψ0 in the unfavourable case and T_1 with 0.8.. For a combination which uses ADD it is also possible to input together actions and action groups. For example it is useful, if a specific variable action is the leading variable action and all other defined variable actions are the accompanying variable actions. With the input:.
 COMB 1 EXPL TYPE DESI
 ADD {G} FACU GAMU FACF GAMF ADD W FACU 1.5 FACF 0.0
 ADD {QI} FACU PSIU FACF 0.0
 all permanent actions (action group {G}) are combined with the leading variable action W and all other variable actions as accomanying variable actions (action group {QI}).
 You can find further explanations and examples for the explicit defined combinations in our Online Help -> Tutorials
 https://www.sofistik.de/documentation/2025/en/tutorials/superpositions/superposition.html
Simplified superpositions are described for German DIN 18800 and Austrian OENORM 4300.

The German DIN 18800, the Austrian OENORM 4300, the Russian SNIP and other design codes include a simplified superposition with partial safety factors for the ultimate limit state check:
 either: consideration of only one variable action Q with the partial safety factor γ
 S = γg · Gk ⊕ γq,1 · Qk,1
 (2.8)
 or: consideration of all variable actions Q with the partial safety factors γ · ψ (e.g. for German DIN 18800 = 1.5 · 0.9 = 1.35)
 $$Sv =Yg-Gk(r) > Yq,i Yq.it Qk,i (2.9)$$
 Both superpositions have to be analysed according to the design code. Only the most un- favourable superposition is decisive. MAXIMA processes internally both equations and output, however, only the more unfavourable superposition.
 If an action with type seismic action (E) is available, then this action is processed with equation (8) and (9) because an explicit superposition with seismic combination is not planned here.

metadata.sections: 2.4.1 Ultimate Limit State Check: Fundamental Combination

content:
The simplified superposition for the accidental combination is only allowed for German DIN 18800 and Austrian OENORM 4300.
 For accidental combinations according to German DIN 18800 and Austrian OENORM 4300 the permanent actions G are used, however, with γg = 1.0 and all variable actions Q, however, with γ = 0.9 (= 0.9 · 1.0) according to the equations 2.8 and 2.9. Additionally the accidental action FA is considered as follows:
 FA,d = γF · F,k
 (2.10)
 with γF = 1.0

content: For a superposition of non-linearly analysed load cases an envelope is formed. Only load cases without factors are superimposed here and only one decisive load case is determined. The superposition of non-linearly analysed load cases is only permitted, if the load cases are defined via alternative groups (record LC type AG1) or if the calculation occurred with a linearised calculation according to OENORM. If using the literal NONL for EXTR in record COMB, the load cases are processed automatically with TYPE AG1. It is to be noted here, that no action (no record ACT) has to be entered in MAXIMA even if the defined design code prescribes actions for superpositions after linear calculations.

content: For special projects it can be necessary to execute an intermediate superposition. The deter- mined result load cases of an intermediate superposition can be used then as initial load cases for further combinations. For an intermediate superposition it is also possible here to assign the result load cases with COMB TYPE to an action which was defined before in SOFiLOAD.

When using load groups with ACT PART Q_1 till Q_99 it is possible to make intermediate superpositions internally within a MAXIMA run, e.g. for relevant traffic loads. The superposition with load groups is shown and described in the example file maxima_loadgroups.dat.
 For comparison the intermediate superposition with explicit MAXIMA definitions is shown in the example file maxima_intermediate-superposition.dat.

The input occurs in a free format with the CADINP input language (see the general manual SOFiSTiK: ’Basics’).
 Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).
 [mm]1011 Implicit unit. Implicit units are categorised semantically and denoted by a cor- responding identity number (shown in green). Valid categories referring to the unit ”length” are, for example, geodetic elevation, section length and thickness. The default unit for each category is defined by the currently active (design code specific) unit set. This input default can be overridden as described above. The specified unit in square brackets corresponds to the default for unit set 5 (Eu- rocodes, NORM UNIT 5).

The table defines a set of MAXIMA “records” (or keywords) together with the fields (“items”) that each record may carry. These records form the building blocks for specifying load combinations, actions, superpositions, tracing and output options within the SOFiMAXIMA environment. In what follows, each record is listed along with its purpose, its available fields, and its relation to the general procedure described in the SOFiSTiK “Basics” manual and to the workflow of SOFiLOAD + MAXIMA.

1. CTRL  
   • Items: OPT, VAL  
   • Purpose: Switches and general control parameters. OPT selects an option mode or keyword; VAL assigns a numerical or logical value.

2. COMB  
   • Items: NO, EXTR, BASE, TYPE, COMC, TITL  
   • Purpose: Defines a combination rule.  
     – NO: combination number or identifier  
     – EXTR: extraction or superposition type (e.g. “EXTR”)  
     – BASE: reference combination number or base group  
     – TYPE: standard, explicit, design, etc.  
     – COMC: combination code (e.g. “EXTR DESI”)  
     – TITL: user‐supplied title for documentation  

3. ACT  
   • Items: TYPE, GAMU, GAMF, PSI0, PSI1, PSI2, PS1S, PART, SUP, TITL  
   • Purpose: Specification of an action group (loads, partial factors, conversion factors, psi‐factors). Used only when modifications to actions from SOFiLOAD are required.  

4. ADD  
   • Items: TYPE, FACU, FACF  
   • Purpose: Selection of an individual action to add to an explicit combination (used with COMB EXTR EXPL). FACU/FACF are unfactored/factored load intensities.

5. ADA  
   • Items: TYPE  
   • Purpose: (Less commonly used) Records for additional data or advanced definitions.

6. LC  
   • Items: NO, TYPE, FACT  
   • Purpose: Defines a load case. When LC and ACT records are not modified, they need not be re‐entered—in these cases, combinations draw directly on the SOFiLOAD database.

7. SUPP  
   • Items: COMB, EXTR, ETYP, TYPE, FROM, TO, INC, X, SELE, LC, TITL, OPT  
   • Purpose: Defines the superposition of actions and/or load cases within a combination.  
     – COMB, EXTR, ETYP identify which combination and extraction type  
     – TYPE indicates additive or envelope superposition  
     – FROM, TO, INC select ranges of load cases or actions  
     – SELE, X, LC offer more granular inclusion criteria  
     – TITL, OPT allow documentation and option flags

8. SUM  
   • Items: COMB, LC, TITL  
   • Purpose: Summarizes results by combination and load case; TITL adds a heading.

9. EXPO  
   • Items: OPT, TO, PASS  
   • Purpose: Controls export settings, such as the output file name or format, and pass numbers.

10. ECHO  
    • Items: OPT, VAL  
    • Purpose: Controls echoing of input data in the printout (on/off flags, verbosity level).

11. TRAC  
    • Items: LC, ETYP, ELEM, X, SELE, OPT, CSAV  
    • Purpose: Enables “combination tracing” for specified load cases and elements. TRAC must be issued in a separate MAXIMA run after SUPP definitions.  
      – LC: target load case number  
      – ETYP: element type (e.g. BEAM)  
      – ELEM: element identifier  
      – OPT: filter options such as “IF” to trace only those load cases actually contributing  
      – CSAV: controls saving of the trace summary  

General Usage Notes  
• HEAD, END and PAGE records frame each MAXIMA run  
• COMB and SUPP are mandatory whenever new superposition schemes are defined  
• ACT and LC records are optional if no changes to existing actions or load cases are needed  
• Explicit combinations (COMB EXTR EXPL) use ADD and LC to pick and modify individual actions before SUPP  
• Standard combinations (COMB EXTR STAN) may omit ACT and rely directly on load cases (LC)  
• TRAC records must follow SUPP in a fresh run to produce element‐level load case tracing.

This table presents a concise mapping of six fundamental load-combination categories defined in the Swiss standard SIA 260 (often grouped under the broader SIA 26X series) to their respective shorthand codes (“COMB EXTR”). Such a mapping is critical for structural-design workflows, enabling engineers, software tools, and document repositories to reference combination definitions unambiguously and to support downstream processes like automated checks, report generation, or RAG-style retrieval in a vector store.

   • “COMB EXTR”  
     – Abbreviated code used to tag or extract the corresponding combination type in databases, spreadsheets, BIM platforms, or design scripts.

2. Rows and Their Significance  
   1. Design fundamental combination SIA 260 → EXPL  
      • “EXPL” stands for the principal (or explicit) combination applied during ultimate-limit-state verifications. It usually encompasses permanent loads with variable actions at their characteristic values.  
   2. Accidental combination SIA 260 → ACCI  
      • “ACCI” indicates an accidental load scenario, such as impacts or abnormal overloads (e.g., vehicle collision). These combinations use reduced factors for unforeseeable effects.  
   3. Seismic combination SIA 260 → EARQ  
      • “EARQ” is reserved for earthquake-induced loads. Seismic combinations typically modify permanent and variable actions with specific partial factors and include inertial forces.  
   4. Characteristic (rare) combination SIA 260 → RARE  
      • “RARE” denotes a rare (characteristic) variable-action combination used for serviceability checks where a single variable action may reach its characteristic peak.  
   5. Frequent combination equation SIA 260 → FREQ  
      • “FREQ” applies to frequently occurring load patterns in serviceability-limit-state checks, capturing realistic operational conditions over time.  
   6. Quasi-permanent combination equation SIA 260 → PERM  
      • “PERM” addresses long-term effects where variable actions are represented by their quasi-permanent values (e.g., sustained live load fractions for creep and shrinkage analyses).

3. Contextual Notes for RAG Vector Store Integration

The table under consideration is drawn from the suite of Eurocode loading combination provisions (BS EN 1990 and its bridge-specific counterpart BS EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE). It catalogues the principal combination equations prescribed by EN 1990 (clause numbers in parentheses) and assigns each one a short alphanumeric code (“COMB”) for easy reference in a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) or vector-search context. The layout comprises two columns:

 1. Combination  
    – The full title of the combination equation together with the Eurocode clause reference in parentheses.  
 2. COMB  
    – A four-character shorthand label used to index or tag that combination in downstream retrieval or explanation modules.

Below is a breakdown of each row:

• Design fundamental combination equation (6.10) EN 1990 → DESI  
  This is the core “ultimate limit state” (ULS) form for fundamental combinations of variable actions with permanent actions. It represents the principal load scenario used to verify strength and stability.

• Design fundamental combination equation (6.10a/6.10b) EN 1990 → EXPL  
  An “explicit” variant of the fundamental combination that splits leading and accompanying variable actions into separate factors (ψ0 and ψ1).

• Accidental combination equation (6.11b) EN 1990 with leading variable action ψ₁,₁ · Q_k,1 → ACCI  
  The accidental-action formula incorporating the full characteristic leading variable action. Used to check structural resistance under infrequent but credible accidental loads (e.g. vehicle collision, impact).

• Accidental combination equation (6.11b) EN 1990 without leading variable action ψ₂,₁ · Q_k,1 → EXPL  
  An alternate “explicit” form where the accidental leading action is reduced by its association factor ψ₂,₁, reflecting less conservative simultaneous occurrence of other loads.

• Seismic combination equation (6.12b) EN 1990 → EARQ  
  The “earthquake” combination for ULS under seismic excitation. It includes the design seismic action combined with reduced permanent and variable loads.

• Characteristic (rare) combination equation (6.14b) EN 1990 → RARE  
  A serviceability-limiting form combining characteristic values of frequent variable actions with permanent loads, used for “rare” long-term checks.

• Frequent combination equation (6.15b) EN 1990 → FREQ  
  Applies reduced values of variable actions (ψ₁ factors) reflecting “frequent” loading scenarios relevant to fatigue and long-term deflection assessments.

• Quasi-permanent combination equation (6.16b) EN 1990 → PERM  
  Emphasizes lasting (“permanent”) load effects by applying quasi-permanent factors ψ₂ to variable actions; used for deformation and long-term stress checks.

• Infrequent combination equation (A2.1b) EN 1990 → NONF  
  An “infrequent” combination from Annex A, often used for bridge structures (BS EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE) to capture less common load interactions without full ULS conservatism.

By indexing these nine key combinations with concise codes (DESI, EXPL, ACCI, EARQ, RARE, FREQ, PERM, NONF), the table provides a standardized taxonomy for rapid lookup, filtering, and cross-referencing within a RAG vector store. Each code succinctly encapsulates not only the type of combination (e.g. seismic vs. accidental) but also its underlying Eurocode reference, facilitating automated retrieval of definitions, formulae, and design checks across the BS EN 199X-200X family.

Explanation of Columns  
• Combination (Column 1): This column enumerates the main categories of load and action combinations as defined in Eurocode standards.  
  – Design fundamental combinations: The principal sets of loads and actions (dead, live, wind, snow, etc.) combined according to partial coefficients for ultimate limit state checks.  
  – Accidental combinations: Load scenarios accounting for rare or exceptional events (impact, vehicle collision, structural element loss, etc.).  
  – Combinations for serviceability limit state: Configurations of loads used to verify deflections, vibrations, crack widths and other serviceability criteria under normal usage conditions.

• COMB EXTR (Column 2): This column indicates how each combination type should be handled or tagged when populating the RAG vector store. The code “EXPL” stands for “explicit extraction,” implying that every instance or definition of these combinations should be directly and unambiguously extracted from the source text. In practice, this ensures that queries related to any of these three combination types can retrieve well-structured, standalone records in the vector index.

Contextual Notes  
• BS EN199X-200X and BS EN199X-200X-BRIDGE are placeholders for the various Eurocode parts (e.g., EN 1990 through EN 1999 and their bridge-dedicated counterparts). They collectively cover general principles, actions, design rules for buildings, geotechnical design, seismic design, and specialized bridge provisions.  
• In a knowledge-graph or RAG environment, tagging these three combination categories as EXPL means that when text passages in the standards mention “design fundamental combinations,” “accidental combinations,” or “combinations for serviceability limit state,” they should be harvested in full (including accompanying coefficients, clauses, notes) rather than inferred or contextually deduced.

Overall, this table serves as a schema for guiding automated or semi-automated extraction of critical load combination definitions from Eurocode documents, ensuring that each of the fundamental, accidental, and serviceability-relevant scenarios is captured in explicit, machine-readable form.

   • Involves permanent loads plus the quasi-permanent portion of variable actions (long-term value), enabling checks on long-term effects like creep, shrinkage, and sustained deflections.

The table under consideration is a concise summary of the principal load‐combination types used in structural design standards (notably the Eurocodes and Chinese GB standards), along with the abbreviated labels by which they are referenced in design documentation and software.  It contains two columns:  

• Combination – a descriptive name for each class of load combination.  
• COMB EXTR – the short code or label (EXPL, RARE, FREQ, PERM) that a design office or calculation package might use to flag which combination rule is being applied.  

Below is a breakdown of each row in the table, explaining its role in a structural safety assessment:  

1. Design fundamental combinations (EXPL)  
   • Description: These are the primary “ultimate limit state” combinations in which permanent loads (dead loads), variable loads (live loads, wind, snow), and environmental actions are factored by their partial safety coefficients and combination factors. They represent the most onerous scenario for strength verification.  
   • Code: EXPL, shorthand for “explicit” or “explorative” checks, indicating that the combination’s factors are explicitly laid out in the standard’s clauses.  
   • Typical use: Checking bending moments, shear forces, and axial forces in beams, slabs, columns under near–worst‐case load mixes.  

2. Accidental combinations (EXPL)  
   • Description: These account for rare accidental actions (e.g. vehicle impact, explosions, fire-induced thermal gradients) in combination with other loads. The design philosophy treats the accidental action as quasi‐random and applies special partial factors.  
   • Code: EXPL (same code as design fundamental, because these combinations are similarly prescribed in the standard).  
   • Typical use: Verifying the residual strength of structural elements subject to unintended load scenarios or impact events.  

3. Characteristic (rare) combination (RARE)  
   • Description: Composed of the most unfavourable (or characteristic) values of permanent actions plus a single variable action at its characteristic (frequently the 95th percentile) value, with other variable actions at reduced values. Used for serviceability checks—particularly when assessing deflection or crack width under long‐term loading.  
   • Code: RARE, emphasizing that only one variable action is at its full characteristic magnitude while others are “rarely” at their maximum simultaneously.  
   • Typical use: Long‐term deflection, crack‐width control in reinforced concrete members (e.g. under a heavy live‐load pattern plus self‐weight).  

4. Frequent combination (FREQ)  
   • Description: This combination includes permanent loads and the “frequent” values of variable actions, defined by the standard’s combination factors (e.g. ψ2 factors). It is intended to check phenomena that develop under moderately high but not extreme loads—such as fatigue, vibration comfort, or service limit states.  
   • Code: FREQ, indicating that variable actions are scaled to their frequent occurrence intensity.  
   • Typical use: Verifying vibration amplitudes in floor systems under walking loads or fatigue checks for steel connections.  

5. Quasi‐permanent combination (PERM)  
   • Description: Permanent actions plus variable actions reduced to their long‐term (quasi‐permanent) values (ψ3 factors). It addresses effects that depend on the sustained level of loading—creep, shrinkage, long‐term settlement or loss of prestress.  
   • Code: PERM, underlining that the loads are those that persist for the majority of the structure’s life.  
   • Typical use: Assessing time‐dependent deformations in concrete beams or long‐term camber in prestressed members.  

Contextual references:  
• NBN EN 199X-200X, NBN EN 199X-200X-BRIDGE – European harmonized standards (Eurocode series), including bridge provisions, define these combination rules in clauses on limit state design.  
• GB 50010-2010, GB 50010 – Chinese Standard for concrete design also follows a similar schema of combination categories, albeit with slightly different partial factors and nomenclatures.  

In a retrieval‐augmented generation (RAG) workflow, this table can serve as a metadata lookup: whenever a structural model or user query refers to EXPL, FREQ, RARE or PERM combinations, the system can automatically expand the shorthand to its full descriptive context, fetch the relevant formulae and partial factors from the appropriate standard, and ensure consistency across multilingual or multi‐standard projects.

The input table defines two related records—OPT and VAL—that together control how MAXIMA’s initialization (INI) defaults are applied and how intermediate results and combination data are managed in the calculation database. Below is a breakdown of every column and row, plus an explanation of how each field is used in context with the surrounding CTRL method of calculation.

1. Columns  
  • Item  
    – The name of the record being defined (OPT or VAL).  
  • Description  
    – A human-readable explanation of the record’s purpose and its sub-options (for OPT), or of the values allowed (for VAL).  
  • Unit  
    – The data type or format expected. “LIT” indicates a literal (flag or keyword). A dash (“–”) means no specific unit/type.  
  • Default  
    – The value assumed if the user does not explicitly specify one.

2. Record OPT (Unit = LIT)  
  This record groups three binary (0/1) switches that affect:  
  – whether results are stored,  
  – whether newly defined load cases are deleted,  
  – whether combination rules and superposition commands are cleared.  
  By issuing “CTRL OPT …” in a MAXIMA input block (e.g. within a PROG MAXIMA … END section), you override or confirm the INI-file defaults.

  Sub-options under OPT:  
  A) SAVE  
    • Purpose: Controls how results of the current run are handled.  
      – 0 = print only (do not save to database)  
      – 1 = store in database (default)  
    • Typical use: turn off saving if you only need a quick one-off printout.  
  B) DELE  
    • Purpose: Defines whether any newly defined load cases in the current run are erased before the next execution.  
      – 0 = do not delete newly defined cases  
      – 1 = delete newly defined cases (default)  
    • Context: only meaningful if prior runs have already populated the database. If you set DELE = 0, the program assumes all required node/element results already exist from a previous run; otherwise you risk “No. −3 in MUDS” errors when overlapping records are out of sync.  
  C) INIT  
    • Purpose: Clears all combination rules and superposition commands from the database.  
      – 0 = do not delete (default)  
      – 1 = delete  
    • Note: As of version 2026 this flag is obsolete. Deletion of combination data is now handled through SSD/TEDDY’s Database Tools → Database clean menu.  
    • Use case: you might set INIT = 1 if you want to recalculate a series of MAXIMA blocks from scratch—without fully wiping out other stored results.

3. Record VAL (Unit = –, Default = *)  
  This record simply captures whether a given option is activated or not. It takes one of two literal values:  
  – YES = the option is applied  
  – NO = the option is not applied  
  By coupling “OPT” with “VAL,” the user can say, for example:  
   CTRL OPT SAVE VAL YES  
  to explicitly request that results be stored (even though SAVE’s default is already 1).

4. How It Fits into CTRL (Method of Calculation)  
  In section 3.5 of the documentation, CTRL is introduced as the overarching command for customizing the run behavior.  
  – If you omit CTRL entirely, none of these fine-tuning options is applied (“option is not used”).  
  – CTRL DELE NO is the minimal setting that preserves only the data from the current run, assuming a full database already exists.  
  – CTRL INIT lets you drop combination rules on demand, which is useful for iterative design checks when you don’t want to flush out all other results.

Together, OPT and VAL form a small but powerful schema for controlling data persistence, cleanup, and re-execution behavior in SOFiSTiK’s MAXIMA environment.

sections: 3.4 Usage of Defaults from INI File

content:
With the input
 PROG MAXIMA
 HEAD ECHO ... $(not urgently necessary)$ END
 the defaults of the INI file are activated for the selected design code. Precondition for this is the usage of the preset actions of the record ACT (SOFiLOAD).
 3.5 CTRL – Method of Calculation
 CTRL
 NO
 Option is not used.
 An input for DELE only makes sense, if not all elements or nodes were selected and results have already been stored. With CTRL DELE NO one stipulates that only the data generated in the current program run is stored. However, it is necessary that results for all nodes, elements and beam sections must have already been stored in the database, because the program can not insert anything between two data records.
 If for example two results from a concentrated load have to be stored for a beam section, then they must already be present in the load case which is to be overwritten, otherwise an error message (No. -3 in MUDS) occurs.
 All combination rules and superposition commands which are available in the database are deleted with an input CTRL INIT. Thus it is possible to calculate some MAXIMA input blocks (e.g. with default from the INI file and manual inputs) twice and more without deletion of the complete database.

content:
The input table defines “COMB” records, each of which establishes one structural load-combination rule in the MAXIMA/AQUA workflow.  Every COMB entry consists of five main fields (NO, EXTR, BASE, TYPE, TITL), and must be followed—unless explicitly skipped—by action (ACT), additive (ADD/ADA) and load-case (LC) records that detail which loads participate in that combination.  Below is a field-by-field description, together with key usage notes and cross-references.

1. NO (Number of the combination)  
   • Integer index from 1 to 999   
   • Internally stored as multiples of 100 (minimum 100, maximum 999 900)  
   • Default: –1 (undefined)  
   • Purpose: uniquely identifies one preset combination (read from INI file or defined interactively)  
   • See also record SUPP for supplemental information on numbering

2. EXTR (Kind of superposition / design-code category)  
   • Specifies which design code combination rule applies:  
     DESI   → Design fundamental combination  
     ACCI   → Design accidental combination (leading variable action ψ₁,₁·Qₖ,₁)  
     EARQ   → Design seismic combination  
     PERM   → Serviceability permanent combination  
     RARE   → Serviceability characteristic (rare) combination  
     FREQ   → Serviceability frequent combination  
     NONF   → Serviceability infrequent combination  
     DESI-V → Simplified fundamental combination  
     ACCI-V → Simplified accidental combination  
     RARE-V → Simplified rare combination  
     STAN   → Standard combination (no partial safety factors or combination coefficients)  
     NONL   → Nonlinear load-case combination  
     EXPL   → Explicitly defined combination (must use ADD/ADA next, ACT not allowed)  
   • Unit: none  
   • Default: DESI, ACCI, EARQ, PERM, RARE, FREQ, NONF or STAN (depending on code)

3. BASE (Base load case number)  
   • Identifies the primary load case from which this combination derives  
   • Must be a multiple of 100 (same range as NO)  
   • Default: –1 (unspecified)  
   • Unit: none

4. TYPE (Type of the result load cases)  
   • Classifies how load cases should be handled or grouped when this combination is evaluated:  
     H    → Primary loads only  
     HZ   → Primary plus additional loads  
     NONE → No assignment (EN 1995 / DIN 1052 timber default)  
     PT   → Permanent combination  
     LT   → Long-term combination  
     MT   → Middle-term combination  
     ST   → Short-term combination  
     VT   → Very short-term (accidental)  
     FIRE → Fire scenario combination  
     COMC → Copying rule (generates a derived combination, allows EXTR/BASE changes)  

5. TITL (Designation of the combination)  
   • Free-text name or label for the rule (up to Lt32 characters)  
   • Helps users identify purpose, e.g. “Ultimate Wind + Dead” or “Seismic Check”

Usage Notes and Workflow Integration  
– A COMB record must precede the set of ACT/ADD/ADA and LC records that actually assign actions (loads) to the combination.  If no such records follow, MAXIMA applies default action and load-case assignments.  
– Actions must be pre-defined in SOFiLOAD (via record ACT) and may only be modified with ACT in MAXIMA.  For explicit combinations (EXPL), users must define action sets exclusively with ADD and ADA—ACT records are disallowed after COMB … EXPL.  
– The design code (Eurocode, American code, etc.) is chosen at the start of a session (record NORM in AQUA or via SSD system information).  COMB picks up that code to interpret EXTR, TYPE defaults and combination coefficients.  
– See also:  
  • ACT  (defines individual load actions)  
  • ADD/ADA  (groups or weights actions for explicit combinations)  
  • LC   (assigns individual load cases to actions)  
  • SUPP (supplemental settings for numbering, units, etc.)

See also: ACT, ADD, LC, SUPP
 COMB

 A combination rule is selected with COMB. In general the action effects (record ACT or ADD and ADA) with their relevant load cases (record LC) relate to this rule. The actions and the load cases which are a part of the respective combination are to be input behind the corresponding COMB record! Otherwise the default of the actions and load cases is activated. The actions have to be already available in the database (definition in program SOFiLOAD) and can be only modified in MAXIMA with the record ACT. It is also possible to define combinations without actions.

The actions and the load cases which are a part of the respective combination are to be input behind the corresponding COMB record! Otherwise the default of the actions and load cases is activated. The actions have to be already available in the database (definition in program SOFiLOAD) and can be only modified in MAXIMA with the record ACT. It is also possible to define combinations without actions..
 MAXIMA takes the design code to be used for the combination rule from the database. The user has to specify the design code right at the beginning of the task, either in the program AQUA (record NORM) or in the case of an interactive input with the SSD at System Informa- tion.
 If using an explicit combination with EXTR EXPL the definition of actions or action groups must follow with the records ADD and ADA. An input of the record ACT after COMB EXTR EXPL is
 not allowed.

This table defines all of the allowed EXTR literals for selecting design-code combination rules in the database, shows each one’s default TYPE mapping, and provides a short description or normative reference (“Meaning”).  The EXTR value ultimately determines which combination rule (and thus which partial safety factors, combination coefficients, etc.) the software will apply when it generates load combinations.  Which EXTR literals are actually permitted for any given design code is controlled by that code’s INI file, and you can override the defaults there if necessary.

Columns  
• EXTR: the user-supplied literal that identifies a particular combination rule  
• Default TYPE: if you omit an explicit TYPE entry, this is the record TYPE the system will assume  
• Meaning: a pointer to the relevant clause and equation in the design standard, or else a brief behavioral description  

Rows

1. DESI  
   – Default TYPE: DESI  
   – Meaning: ultimate limit state combination (“design combination”) as per chapter 2.2.1, equation 2.1  

2. ACCI  
   – Default TYPE: ACCI  
   – Meaning: ultimate limit state accidental action combination, chapter 2.2.2, equation 2.2  

3. EARQ  
   – Default TYPE: EARQ  
   – Meaning: ultimate limit state earthquake combination, chapter 2.2.3, equation 2.3  

4. PERM  
   – Default TYPE: PERM  
   – Meaning: serviceability limit state permanent action combination, chapter 2.2.4, equation 2.7  

5. RARE  
   – Default TYPE: RARE  
   – Meaning: serviceability limit state rare variable action combination, chapter 2.2.4, equation 2.4  

6. FREQ  
   – Default TYPE: FREQ  
   – Meaning: serviceability frequent variable action combination, chapter 2.2.4, equation 2.5  

7. NONF  
   – Default TYPE: NONF  
   – Meaning: serviceability combination with non-frequent variable actions, chapter 2.2.4, equation 2.6  

8. DESI-V  
   – Default TYPE: DESI  
   – Meaning: simplified superposition (e.g. German DIN 18800 or OENORM 4300), see chapter 2.4.1, equations 2.8 & 2.9  

9. ACCI-V  
   – Default TYPE: ACCI  
   – Meaning: simplified accidental superposition (DIN 18800/OENORM 4300 only); chapter 2.4.2, equation 2.10, with γ = 1.0 for permanent (G) & variable (Q)  

10. RARE-V  
    – Default TYPE: RARE  
    – Meaning: simplified rare-variable superposition, chapter 2.4.3, equations 2.11 & 2.12  

11. STAN  
    – Default TYPE: STAN  
    – Meaning: “standard” or unspecified design combination—used when no partial factors or combination coefficients apply (e.g. old DIN 1045)  

12. NONL  
    – Default TYPE: none (must explicitly input TYPE here)  
    – Meaning: non-linear envelope combination; no action factors or combination rules apply, and all input load cases are forced to TYPE AG1 (record LC)  

13. EXPL  
    – Default TYPE: none  
    – Meaning: user-defined explicit combinations, either with individual actions or grouped actions (free‐form)  

Usage notes  
– DESI, ACCI and EARQ are normally used for ultimate limit state checks; PERM, RARE, FREQ and NONF for serviceability.  
– For simplified superpositions under German/OENORM practice you must use the “-V” variants.  The Russian SNIP 2.01.07-85 also supports DESI-V, ACCI (standard) and RARE-V.  
– STAN is a catch-all for codes that do not require any partial factors or combination coefficients.  
– NONL and EXPL require you to supply additional TYPE entries—you cannot rely on defaults.  
– All of these defaults and the set of allowed EXTR literals per design code can be tailored in the code’s INI file.

The combination rule which corresponds to the design code in the database is determined with EXTR. Which of the input literals are allowed for a design code is defined in the INI file of the relevant design code. It is possible to modify the defaults in the INI file.
 DESI, ACCI and EARQ are to use for checks in ultimate limit state and PERM, RARE, FREQ and NONF for checks in serviceability limit state.
 For the simplified superpositions (e.g. German DIN 18800, OENORM 4300) DESI-V, ACCI-V or RARE-V have to be input. The Russian SNIP 2.01.07-85 allows the superpositions DESI-V, ACCI and RARE-V.
 STAN - unspecified design combination should be used for design codes without partial safety factors and combination coefficients (e.g. German DIN 1045 old).
 NONL is planned for a combination with non-linear calculated load cases (determination of an enveloped). Action (record ACT) are not allowed here. The input load cases are considered compulsorily with TYPE AG1 in record LC.
 In the following table the input possibilities for EXTR are printed with the relevant defaults for TYPE:
 EXTR
 Default for TYPE
 Meaning
 (userdefined)
 EXTR
 Default for TYPE
 Meaning
 (TYPE must be explicitly input here)

The type of the result load cases are defined with TYPE. The defaults for TYPE are defined in the INI file and can be modified there.
 With that it is also possible to use the result load cases for further superposition. The literals which exist in record ACT can be used here for TYPE for an intermediate superposition. In this case it is to be noted that the action has be defined already with a record ACT in program SOFiLOAD. The definition of a new action is not possible in record COMB.
 For design codes without partial safety factors and combination coefficients (e.g. German DIN 1045 old) and for German DIN 1052 also STAN - general design combination, H - primary loads or HZ - primary and additional loads can be input.
 With the EN 1995 (EC5) and the derived design codes correction factors kmod have been introduced for the permissible stresses and kdeƒ for the deformations. The distinct value is depending not only on the material but also on the service class and the duration of the loading. The information about the duration of the loading has to be available at the superposition load cases. This is done via an input of PT, LT, MT, ST or VT for TYPE.
 If using a free defined combination rule with EXTR EXPL or the combination of non-linear calculated load cases with EXTR NONL, the type of the resultant load cases must be explicitly defined.

content:
The table is the definition of the ACT‐record in SOFiLOAD/MAXIMA, i.e. the parameters that describe one “action” (load or combination of loads) in the structural‐analysis database.  Each row names one input field, gives a short description, its data‐type or unit and whether it must be supplied (“!”) or has a default (“*”).  Below is a field‐by‐field breakdown including the allowable enumerations for those fields that take coded values.

1. TYPE  
   • Description: 4‐character literal identifying the action (e.g. “G”, “Q_1”, “S”, “WIND”).  
   • Unit/Data‐type: LIT4 (literal up to 4 characters).  
   • Default: none – must be supplied (“!”).  
   • Notes: Subcategories are appended with underscore and letter(s) (e.g. “Q_A”).  Certain combinations (reserved codes) are defined in the INI for each design code.

2. GAMU  
   • Description: unfavourable (strength‐reducing) partial safety factor γ<sub>G</sub> or γ<sub>Q</sub>.  
   • Unit: dimensionless (–).  
   • Default: inherited from the INI‐file (“*”).

3. GAMF  
   • Description: favourable (strength‐increasing) partial safety factor.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: from INI.

4. PSI0  
   • Description: combination coefficient for rare combinations (ψ<sub>0</sub>).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: from INI.

5. PSI1  
   • Description: combination coefficient for frequent combinations (ψ<sub>1</sub>).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: from INI.

6. PSI2  
   • Description: combination coefficient for quasi‐permanent combinations (ψ<sub>2</sub>).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: from INI.

7. PS1S  
   • Description: infrequent combination coefficient (ψ<sub>1s</sub>) – used in some codes for specific load types.  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: from INI.

8. GAMA  
   • Description: partial safety factor for accidental actions (γ<sub>A</sub>).  
   • Unit: –  
   • Default: from INI.

9. PART  
   • Description: identifies which “partition” of the limit‐state superposition equation this action belongs to.  That is, which group in the standard combination formula (EN 1990 §6) the action is assigned.  
   • Unit/Data‐type: LIT (literal).  
   • Default: from INI.  
   • Allowed values:  
     – G  : permanent actions  
     – P  : prestress  
     – Q  : variable actions (all groups)  
     – Q_1 … Q_99 : variable action load group 1 … 99  
     – A  : accidental actions  
     – E  : seismic actions  
   • Notes: If omitted for a user‐defined TYPE it defaults to Q (variable).

10. SUP  
    • Description: default superposition (combination) rule for the load cases belonging to this action.  Governs whether cases are summed, taken conditionally, or exclude each other.  
    • Unit/Data‐type: LIT  
    • Default: from INI.  
    • Allowed values:  
      – PERM : permanent, unique factor (all cases share same γ)  
      – PERC : permanent, individual factors per load case  
      – COND : conditional – only unfavourable contributions  
      – EXCL : mutually exclusive within each category  
      – EXEX : mutually exclusive within the entire action  
      – UNSI : conditional with sign change (e.g. seismic, wind)  
      – USEX : exclusive with sign change  
      – ALEX : always applied but exclusive within action  
    • Notes: Historic MAXIMA synonyms exist (EXCL ↔ Ano, etc.).  User may override per‐load‐case.

11. TITL  
    • Description: up to 24‐character text label of the action (human‐readable name).  
    • Unit/Data‐type: LIT24  
    • Default: from INI.  

How it fits into workflow (context from ACT/LC text):  
– When a design code is selected in AQUA, its INI‐file feeds default ACT records into SOFiLOAD.  
– Defining an ACT record creates a local copy which can be tweaked (γ factors, ψ values).  
– On creating a load case (LC record), those factors propagate unless overridden.  
– PART ensures correct placement in the limit‐state superposition (G, P, Q, A or E).  
– SUP prescribes whether load cases within an action are summed, chosen conditionally, or mutually exclusive.  
– Categories (sub‐codes) let users distinguish, e.g., different traffic loads (Q_1 vs. Q_2) or wind directions, each with their own γ and ψ values and combination logic.  
– User‐defined actions must supply TYPE and PART; other fields default but should be reviewed against the selected code.

The image is a simple, monochrome “tree-diagram” showing how actions, their categories and associated load cases are organized under a set of defaults (for example, those coming from an INI-File or the Eurocode default settings). All elements are drawn as plain rectangular boxes connected by straight, single‐line branches. No shading or colors are used—everything is rendered in black outline on white background.

At the very top left of the diagram sits the text label “INI-File/ EC-Defaults.” From just to the right of that label, a single vertical line drops down to a horizontal branch that forks to two major action‐type boxes.

1. The upper branch leads to a box labeled “action G.”  
   • Directly beneath “action G,” a short vertical stem splits into two parallel horizontal branches, each ending in an identically styled box labeled “loadcase.”  
   • These two load-case boxes sit side by side, at the same vertical level, indicating that both are child load cases belonging to the permanent action G.

2. The lower branch continues further down to a box labeled “action Q.”  
   • From “action Q,” a vertical stem extends downward and then bifurcates into two sub-branches, each feeding into one of two category boxes:  
     a) On the left is “action Q_A.” From this Q_A box another short vertical branch splits into two “loadcase” boxes arranged side by side.  
     b) On the right is “action Q_B.” In exactly the same fashion, a short stem under Q_B divides into two identical “loadcase” boxes.

All text labels in the boxes use the same simple sans-serif font. The layout uses consistent box sizes for the action boxes and slightly smaller identical boxes for each load case. Branch lines are straight, meet neatly at right angles where needed, and are of uniform stroke width. The entire graphic occupies the central portion of the image against a white background, with plenty of whitespace around it. Below the diagram (just visible at the bottom edge) sits a caption—partially cut off—that reads: “Figure …: Structure of the actions, their categories and their load cases.”

Overall, the diagram conveys a three-level hierarchy:  
– Level 1: The source of defaults (“INI-File/ EC-Defaults”).  
– Level 2: Two primary actions (G and Q).  
– Level 3: Under G, two load cases; under Q, two categories (Q_A and Q_B), each of which has two load cases of its own. This neatly illustrates how variable and permanent actions are subdivided into categories and down to individual load cases in the software’s default configuration.

The input table provides a compact overview of the preset “action” (load) types available in SOFiLOAD/MAXIMA, showing for each action its normal code (TYPE), its “additional” variant (prefixed Z …), its “special” variant (prefixed S …) and a short descriptive remark. These alphanumeric codes (up to four characters) correspond to the ACT‐record TYPE in MAXIMA and link back to default partial safety factors (GAMU/GAMF) and combination coefficients (ψ‐values) defined in the design‐code INI‐files.  

Column definitions  
• Normal: the primary literal identifying the action group.  
• Add.: code for “additional” loads of the same group (prefix Z). These loads are treated as additive superposition cases.  
• Spec.: code for “special” loads (prefix S), often used for service‐ or design‐level variants.  
• Remark: human‐readable description of the load action.  

Row-by-row summary  
  – NONE (–/–/–): load case not assigned to any action.  
  – G ᵍ, ZG ᵍ, SG ᵍ: total dead load (permanent). Internally G_1 and G_2 sum here.  
  – G_1 ᵍ, Z1 ᵍ, S1 ᵍ: primary dead load (always added).  
  – G_2 ᵍ, Z2 ᵍ, S2 ᵍ: secondary dead load (always added).  
  – P ᵍ, ZP ᵍ, SP ᵍ: prestress effects (for older DIN codes use V).  
  – C ᵍ, ZC ᵍ, SC ᵍ: creep and shrinkage.  
  – Q ᵠ, ZQˣ, SQˣ: generic variable (live) load.  
  – Lˣ, ZLˣ, SLˣ: life load. In analog mode L_T (movable loads, TS) or ZL for UDL (uniformly distributed load).  
  – Wˣ, ZWˣ, SWˣ: wind loading (use ZW for bridge‐specific wind).  
  – Sᵠ, ZSˣ, SSˣ: snow loading (use ZS for bridges).  
  – Rᵍ, ZRˣ, SRˣ: earth pressure or hydrostatic water pressure.  
  – Fᵠ, ZFˣ, SFˣ: settlements (ZF = expected, SF = possible).  
  – Tˣ, ZTˣ, STˣ: temperature effects.  
  – Aˣ, ZAˣ, SAˣ: accidental actions.  
  – Bˣ, ZBˣ, SBˣ: construction/maintenance (ZB = bearing resistance check; SB = bearing exchange).  
  – Eˣ, ZEˣ, SEˣ: seismic actions (ZE = service‐level, SE = design‐level).  

Key points and context  
• The superscript “g” flags permanent actions (SUP = PERM by default, PART = G). These are always included in combinations.  
• Actions with leading Q (variable) default to SUP = COND (conditionally added if unfavorable) and PART = Q.  
• Actions with leading Z or S are simply alternate coding for additional or special superposition rules but belong to the same PART group as their normal counterpart.  
• In MAXIMA the user can override the default PART (permanent, variable, accidental or seismic) and SUP (PERM, PERC, COND, EXCL, EXEX, ALEX) for each load case or combine cases across groups using LC records.  
• This table thus serves as the mapping reference between the shorthand TYPE codes in ACT records and their engineering meaning, ensuring consistent assignment of partial safety factors and combination rules across SOFi-tools.

The table is a concise catalogue of variable (“Q” and “L”) and accidental (“S”) actions – each further subdivided into categories – together with the ψ-factors ψ₀, ψ₁ and ψ₂ that govern combination rules in limit‐state analyses (per EN 1990, SIA 260, etc.).  These factors are used in the RAG vector store to retrieve, index and combine load cases correctly under the SOFiLOAD / MAXIMA workflow.  

1. Column Headings  
 • Action  
 • ψ₀ (combination coefficient for accompanying variable actions)  
 • ψ₁ (coefficient for following variable actions)  
 • ψ₂ (coefficient for combination with other variable actions)  

2. Action “Q”: Payload for buildings (PART Q)  
 • Q_A Housing  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.50, ψ₂ = 0.30  
 • Q_B Offices  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.50, ψ₂ = 0.30  
 • Q_C Assembly rooms  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.70, ψ₂ = 0.60  
 • Q_D Sales rooms  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.70, ψ₂ = 0.60  
 • Q_E Storage rooms  
   – ψ₀ = 1.00, ψ₁ = 0.90, ψ₂ = 0.80  

3. Action “Q”: Live load for buildings  
 • Q_F Truck load < 30 kN  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.70, ψ₂ = 0.60  
 • Q_G 30 kN < truck load < 160 kN  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.50, ψ₂ = 0.30  
 • Q_H Roofs  
   – ψ₀ = 0.00, ψ₁ = 0.00, ψ₂ = 0.00  

4. Action “L”: Live loads according to EN 1990 (PART Q by default; user may reassign PART Q or PART Q_x)  
 • L_T Tandem axle of LM 1 (γ = 1.35) – “GR_T”  
   – ψ₀ = 0.75, ψ₁ = 0.75, ψ₂ = 0.00  
 • L_U UDL of LM 1 (γ = 1.35) – “GR_U”  
   – ψ₀ = 0.40, ψ₁ = 0.40, ψ₂ = 0.00  
 • L_C Load model UIC 71 (γ = 1.45)  
   – ψ₀ = 0.80, ψ₁ = 0.80, ψ₂ = 0.00  
 • L_D Load model SW/0 (γ = 1.45)  
   – ψ₀ = 0.80, ψ₁ = 0.80, ψ₂ = 0.00  
 • L_E Load model SW/2 (γ = 1.20)  
   – ψ₀ = 0.00, ψ₁ = 1.00, ψ₂ = 0.00  

5. Action “L”: Live load for buildings (alternative to “Q”)  
 • L_F Truck load < 30 kN  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.70, ψ₂ = 0.60  
 • L_G 30 kN < truck load < 160 kN  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.50, ψ₂ = 0.30  
 • L_H Roofs  
   – ψ₀ = 0.00, ψ₁ = 0.00, ψ₂ = 0.00  

6. Action “S”: Snow for buildings (PART Q or PART Q_x if redefined)  
 • S_L Buildings up to 1 000 m elevation  
   – ψ₀ = 0.50, ψ₁ = 0.20, ψ₂ = 0.00  
 • S_H Buildings above 1 000 m elevation  
   – ψ₀ = 0.70, ψ₁ = 0.50, ψ₂ = 0.20  
 • SIA 260 alternative:  
   – ψ₀ = (1 – 60/h), ψ₁ = (1 – 250/h), ψ₂ = (1 – 1 000/h) where h is elevation  

Key points for RAG indexing and MAXIMA/ACT usage:  
 • TYPE (e.g. “Q”, “L”, “S”) identifies the literal used in ACT records (up to 4 chars).  
 • PART assigns the action to a superposition group (G, P, Q, Q_x, A, E). By default, Q and L map to PART Q unless overridden.  
 • SUP governs how multiple load cases within an action combine:  
   – PERM, PERC (permanent), COND (conditional), EXCL (mutually exclusive), EXEX (exclusive within an action), ALEX (always but exclusive), etc.  
 • ψ-factors shown here are defaults from design‐code INI files; they are copied into load cases at creation but can be modified per action or per load case in MAXIMA.  

This table functions as a lookup for automated combination rules—each row is a vector entry keyed by (TYPE, category) with payload ψᵢ values. When building RAG-style queries (e.g. ACT Q_A or ACT L_U), these ψ-entries are retrieved, and the LC records inherit them, ensuring correct partial‐factor application under EN 1990 and related codes.

The table summarizes the standard combination (“ψ”) factors to be used when superimposing variable (non‐permanent) actions in limit‐state design (e.g. EN 1990). These ψ‐factors reduce the accompanying (i.e. non‐leading) characteristic values of variable loads according to their type and the combination case (frequent, quasi‐permanent, etc.).  

1. Table structure  
   • Columns:  
     – Action: a short code plus description of the variable load.  
     – ψ₀: combination factor for an accompanying action when another variable action is taken as leading in the ultimate (U.L.S.) or serviceability (S.L.S.) combination (sometimes called the “combination” or “rare” case).  
     – ψ₁: combination factor for the frequent combination case (used in S.L.S. frequent verifications).  
     – ψ₂: combination factor for the quasi‐permanent combination case (used in S.L.S. quasi‐permanent verifications).  

   • Rows:  
     1. W: Wind for buildings  
     2. T: Temperature (no fire) for buildings  
     3. F: Settlements  
     4. Other actions (i.e. all other variable loads not otherwise listed)  

2. Detailed entries  

   1) W: Wind for buildings  
      • ψ₀ = 0.60  
      • ψ₁ = 0.20  
      • ψ₂ = 0.00  
      – Interpretation: If wind is not the leading variable action, its characteristic value is multiplied by 0.60 in the rare combination, by 0.20 in the frequent combination, and by 0.00 in the quasi‐permanent combination (i.e. ignored).  

   2) T: Temperature (no fire) for buildings  
      • ψ₀ = 0.60  
      • ψ₁ = 0.50  
      • ψ₂ = 0.00  
      – Interpretation: Thermal actions (excluding fire) are treated somewhat more persistently than wind; you retain half of their characteristic value in a frequent combination but ignore them in the quasi‐permanent case.  

   3) F: Settlements  
      • ψ₀ = 1.00  
      • ψ₁ = 1.00  
      • ψ₂ = 1.00  
      – Interpretation: Settlement effects are always taken in full—whether as accompanying in the rare, frequent, or quasi‐permanent combination.  

   4) Other actions  
      • ψ₀ = 0.80  
      • ψ₁ = 0.70  
      • ψ₂ = 0.50  
      – Interpretation: All other variable actions (e.g. imposed loads not specifically listed) use these generic reduction factors: 0.80 in the rare combination, 0.70 in the frequent, and 0.50 in the quasi‐permanent.  

3. Usage notes  
   – These ψ‐factors apply to variable actions when they are not chosen as the “leading” action in a combination. The leading action’s full characteristic value is taken (multiplied by 1.0).  
   – In SOFiLOAD/MAXIMA (or any design‐automation process), the ACT record for each variable action will carry its default ψ‐values. If you define subcategories (e.g. Q_A, Q_B, …) or custom actions, you can override these ψ‐values via the ACT command.  
   – The three combination cases correspond to the three standard superposition rules in EN 1990:  
     • ψ₀ – rare / accidental combinations (ultimate limit state)  
     • ψ₁ – frequent combinations (serviceability)  
     • ψ₂ – quasi‐permanent combinations (long‐term effects in serviceability)  

By capturing this table in your vector store, you ensure that any RAG retrieval can immediately supply the correct reduction factors for wind, temperature, settlements, and other variable loads when constructing limit‐state combinations.

 First of all three load groups Q_1, Q_2 and Q_3 are defined with PART in the program SOFiLOAD. The categories XY_A und XY_B are a art of the load group 1. Their load cases are mutually exclusive only within the respective category about the input SUP EXCL. The cate- gories XY_C and XY_D are a part of the load groups 2 and 3. All load cases of both categories are mutually exclusive about the input SUP EXEX.

The categories XY_A und XY_B are a art of the load group 1. Their load cases are mutually exclusive only within the respective category about the input SUP EXCL. The cate- gories XY_C and XY_D are a part of the load groups 2 and 3. All load cases of both categories are mutually exclusive about the input SUP EXEX..
 With one of the MAXIMA combinations then the superposition is done as follows: First of all MAXIMA searches which load cases of the load group 1 are decisive (possible one ore two or no load case = first intermediate superposition).Then the decisive load case of the load groups 2 and 3 is determined (possible one or no load case = second intermediate superposition). In the last step the final superposition is done. Either the decisive load cases of the load group 1 or the decisive load case of the goups 2 and 3 are here the final result.
 It should be noted here that load groups are mutually exclusive. If, for example, the superpo- sition of the load cases for two load load groups are specified with SUP COND - conditionally, only the load cases of the decisive load group are taken into account.

 HEAD

The table shown defines the syntax and semantics of the ADD record, which in SOFiLOAD/COMB workflows is used to assemble explicit combinations of actions and action groups.  It is only valid in conjunction with records COMB, EXTR or EXPL.  Any actions referenced here must have been defined earlier via SOFiLOAD record ACT, and their grouping governed by the PART definition in ACT.  Note also that once you invoke an action group you must not follow with an explicit LC (load-case) record—COMB will automatically generate its associated load cases.  

The table has four columns—Item, Description, Unit, Default—and three rows, one for each parameter of the ADD record:

1.  TYPE  
   •  Unit: LIT4 (four-character literal)  
   •  Default: “!” (mandatory)  
   •  Purpose: Designates which action or action‐group to include in the combination.  You may supply any of the following literal codes enclosed in braces:  
     – {G}   all permanent actions  
     – {P}   all prestress‐and‐creep actions  
     – {Q1}  first leading variable action  
     – {Q2}  second leading variable action  
     – {Q3}  third leading variable action  
     – {Ql}  variable actions, interpreted as:  
         • without any leading action: Ql = all variable actions  
         • with one or more leading Q’s already specified: Ql = remaining variable actions  
     – {A}   all accidental actions  
     – {E}   all seismic actions  

2.  FACU (Unfavourable factor)  
   •  Unit: – / LIT (dimensionless literal or numeric)  
   •  Default: “!” (mandatory)  
   •  Purpose: Defines the unfavourable scaling factor for the chosen action or group.  You may enter either:  
     – a literal number (e.g. 1.35)  
     – or a formula of the form “=factor*literal” (e.g. =1.5*G1)  

3.  FACF (Favourable factor)  
   •  Unit: – / LIT (dimensionless literal or numeric)  
   •  Default: “!” (mandatory)  
   •  Purpose: Defines the favourable scaling factor for the chosen action or group.  Accepts the same formats as FACU: a direct number or “=factor*literal”.

Key Usage Notes:  
• You cannot use ADD to assign a load case (LC) to an action or category—doing so will halt the calculation with an error.  
• If you reference an action group (e.g. {G}, {Q1} …), do not follow ADD with an explicit LC record; the program auto-generates the required load cases.  
• ADD is strictly for explicitly combining previously defined action entries (via ACT) into new COMB records.  

By adhering to these definitions for TYPE, FACU and FACF, you ensure that your combination records are syntactically valid and semantically clear, enabling reliable load combinations in the RAG vector-based workflow.

Below is a structured, RAG-ready description of the single-row table you provided.  It breaks out each column as a field, summarizes its purpose in the overall COMB/ADD/ADA context, and highlights how it’s used when building an action combination record.

1. Table Overview  
   • Purpose: Defines the parameter TYPE within a COMB statement.  
   • Scope: Appears in “COMB … TYPE …” lines to select which action code from a previously defined action group (via ADD/ADA records) will be processed.  

2. Field-by-Field Description  

   – Item  
     • Name: TYPE  
     • Role: Keyword identifying that the following value is the chosen action designation.  
     • Context: In COMB records, this slot tells the system which action (permanent or variable) it should treat as the primary or leading variable action.  

   – Description  
     • Text: “Designation the action from the selected action group”  
     • Interpretation: This field must match one of the action-group labels you’ve assigned in preceding ADD statements (for example G, Q1, QI, etc.).  
     • Integration:  
       1. You define possible action groups (“{G}”, “{Q1}”, “{QI}”) with ADD records.  
       2. You restrict or extend them via ADA records (e.g. ADA Q,S,W to allow only Q, S, or W for that action code).  
       3. The TYPE field picks one label out of that group for the superposition calculation.  

   – Unit  
     • Value: LIT4  
     • Meaning: A four-character literal.  
     • Usage: Ensures the action code is recorded as a fixed-width string (padded or truncated to 4 chars if needed). Common codes include “G”, “Q1”, “QI ” (with trailing spaces), etc.  

   – Default  
     • Symbol: !  
     • Semantics: No implicit default – an exclamation mark forces explicit specification.  
     • Implication: If you omit TYPE or leave it as “!”, the system will flag it as missing and refuse to proceed.  

3. How It Fits in a Typical Input Sequence  

   COMB 1 EXTR EXPL TYPE DESI BASE 2100  
   ADD {G} …  
   ADA G  
   ADD {Q1} …  
   ADA Q,S,W  
   ADD {QI} …  
   ADA Q,S,W  

   – In the above, each ADD/ADA block establishes which action codes are available.  
   – The TYPE slot in COMB picks one of those codes (e.g. TYPE G, TYPE Q1 or TYPE QI) for use in the subsequent superposition.  

4. Key Takeaways for RAG Indexing  
   • “TYPE” is a discrete, required slot: it must be matched exactly against allowed action codes.  
   • LIT4 enforces consistent storage length, making vectorized lookups predictable.  
   • The “!” default underlines the rule that TYPE cannot be omitted – this is crucial when validating or generating COMB records.
